case_studies.title: Prune Gradually, Adapt Sparsely: Efficient Pruning of Large Language Models at Extreme Sparsity
case_studies.abstract: Weight pruning can reduce the storage and inference cost of large language models (LLMs), but preserving quality at high sparsity levels remains challenging. Existing methods face a quality-cost trade-off in this regime. One-shot pruning is cheap but degrades sharply as sparsity increases, even when followed by post-pruning recovery. A growing line of work instead optimizes the mask directly from the dense model under the end-to-end objective; among these methods, [Lee et al.,2026], the recent state of the art at extreme sparsity, reaches high quality but at the cost of model-sized optimizer state and auxiliary variables. To address this gap, we propose ETAPS, which prunes gradually and adapts sparsely: it tightens a global sparsity constraint in progressive stages while training a sparse delta with a small, fixed budget. Our key observation is that gradual weight removal keeps each pruning step small enough for sparse adaptation to compensate, allowing the adapted model to provide end-to-end gradients that guide the next pruning decision without model-sized optimizer state. Across six models from 125M to 13B parameters, ETAPS achieves lower perplexity than ELSA at every evaluated sparsity from 50% to 90%, with perplexity reductions of up to 42%. ETAPS is also far cheaper: at 90% sparsity, it prunes LLaMA2-7B on a single H200, where ELSA uses four, with $5.0\times$ smaller total persistent state and 49% fewer GPU-hours. Together, our findings point to a promising direction for achieving high quality in demanding regimes such as extreme sparsity at substantially lower cost.
case_studies.summary: ETAPS gradually prunes and adapts sparse models, keeping each step small so the model can recover quality without large optimizer states. It outperforms the previous state‑of‑the‑art at 50‑90% sparsity and reduces GPU‑time and memory by up to 49% and 5× respectively. This could help you run cheaper, high‑sparsity LLMs in production.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage large language models, here is what to do: 1) Use ETAPS to prune in stages, 2) Keep the sparse delta small and train it continuously, 3) Monitor perplexity to ensure quality stays above baseline.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a practical algorithm for aggressively pruning large language models while maintaining performance, directly benefiting IT engineers who deploy LLMs in cloud and edge environments. The method claims substantial resource savings and lower GPU usage, making it immediately usable for cost optimisation. The authors report extensive experiments and indicate released code and benchmarks, satisfying the maturity criterion. For monetisation, the approach can be applied to reduce hosting costs or sell as a deployment optimisation service within 90 days. Overall, the work is highly relevant to infrastructure engineers and offers tangible commercial value.

case_studies.title: Context as Infrastructure: Knowledge Compilation for Retrieval in Agentic Systems with Harnesses
case_studies.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation is becoming agentic. A search harness writes queries, reads results, reformulates, and decides when to stop. This largely solves accuracy: a harness with only BM25/grep and MiniMax M3 answers 85% of BrowseComp-Plus and 91% on multi-hop FRAMES in our runs, without compiled or vector indexes. It exposes a context problem: an undisciplined loop repeats queries, rereads documents, and fills the window with unused passages. The missing layer is knowledge compilation: a configurable ingestion pipeline where LLMs enrich documents with context no chunk contains alone--navigation hierarchies with claim-evidence leaves, entity graphs, timelines, mind maps, ontologies, wikis, and memory. Compilation is not a better retriever: under a competent harness, structural artifacts gave no detectable accuracy gain on FRAMES, and a PageIndex-style outline degraded at scale. It is a supply layer. A navigation tree whose leaves are claim-evidence pairs--the mechanism we measure--cuts query tokens by 91% when evidence suffices and adds 1.9% when it does not, a 38% average reduction; this implies a 2% break-even sufficiency rate and a measured rate near 43%. A decision gate cuts latency from 140 s to 30 s, though substitution's token saving is bought with retrieval rounds and carries its own latency cost. Other artifacts--ontology, graph, wiki, timeline, mind map, memory--pay off in deployment (governance, integration, onboarding, temporal orientation, continuity) where accuracy benchmarks cannot see them. We describe RAGFlow's pipeline and harness (open source at https://github.com/infiniflow/ragflow), which turns the loop into five disciplined stations and keeps the context entering the model the smallest sufficient set; together they form an agent-native database: a store that hands the agent compiled, governed context instead of a ranked list of passages.
case_studies.summary: This research shows how to pre‑process and organise knowledge into structured formats (like claim‑evidence trees, entity graphs, timelines) so that an AI agent’s search loop uses only the minimal necessary context, cutting query tokens by 91% and reducing latency from 140s to 30s. The authors built an open‑source pipeline called RAGFlow that turns a chaotic retrieval loop into five disciplined stations, giving the agent a curated, governed context instead of a raw ranked list of passages. For cloud infrastructure managers, this means a way to host and serve structured knowledge bases that improve agent efficiency and governance without adding new retrieval engines.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, set up RAGFlow on your Kubernetes cluster: 1) ingest your documents into the compilation pipeline to generate claim‑evidence trees; 2) expose the compiled store via a REST API; 3) route your agents’ queries through the RAGFlow harness to cut token use and latency.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces an open-source RAGFlow pipeline that restructures retrieval for agentic LLM systems, directly addressing practical infrastructure challenges such as query efficiency, latency, and governance. The solution is immediately deployable with released code and demonstrated performance gains in real-world benchmarks, enabling IT teams to reduce token usage and response times. It offers clear, actionable components (knowledge compilation, decision gating, navigation trees) that can be integrated into existing SaaS and cloud environments, providing a tangible service offering within 90 days. However, the core novelty lies in engineering rather than novel AI research, so scores reflect high practical impact, mature implementation, and moderate monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: SecPO: Principled Adversarial Training for Prompt Injection Security
case_studies.abstract: Recognized as a top threat to AI agents, prompt injection allows instructions from untrusted data (email, documents, websites) to manipulate the agent's operation. The existing best-defended LLM, Meta-SecAlign, is trained with the DPO loss but still suffers from attack success rates (ASRs) approaching 100% under adaptive prompt injections. One reason is that DPO anchors the model around the undefended reference model, which is insecure. We show an idealized reference model---an injection-invariant, utility-preserving oracle---can nevertheless be approximated, as its output distribution in training is interestingly accessible. This new observation motivates a theoretically principled SecPO loss. Another Meta-SecAlign shortcoming is that it trains on weak simulated attacks. We implement an efficient adversarial training (AT) pipeline that synthesizes strong injected inputs (best@240), and train the model on them. Our AT reduces ASRs by 1.5-14.5$\times$ across three SoTA adaptive attacks, compared with Meta-SecAlign; the SecPO loss reduces them by a further 2.4-4.6$\times$ compared with using DPO loss. In agentic workflows, our SecPO + AT Qwen3.6-27B is much more secure than Meta-SecAlign: 8.8% vs. 78.8% AgentDojo ASR@800 under the AttackerMovesSecond attack. Moreover, our defended model shows no noticeable reduction in benign utility in nine benchmarks covering agentic tool calling, instruction following, science, and math. We release our $\href{//github.com/Sizhe-Chen/SecPO}{\text{code}}$, $\href{//huggingface.co/datasets/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO-trainset}{\text{training data}}$ (with optimized injections from AT), and $\href{//huggingface.co/Sizhe-Chen/Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct-SecPO}{\text{model}}$.
case_studies.summary: SecPO introduces a new loss function and adversarial training pipeline that dramatically reduces prompt‑injection attack success rates on LLMs, while keeping normal performance intact. The researchers trained a Qwen‑3.6‑27B model with SecPO and strong synthetic attacks, cutting ASRs 1.5‑14.5× compared to previous methods and 2.4‑4.6× versus standard DPO loss. This shows a practical way to harden AI agents against injection attacks without hurting their usefulness.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted AI services, run the SecPO training code on your models: 1) generate strong injected inputs with their AT pipeline, 2) fine‑tune your model using the SecPO loss, 3) test against known adaptive attacks. This will lower injection success rates and keep service quality high.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete adversarial training framework (SecPO) for protecting LLM-based agents against prompt injection, a real threat in current AI deployments. It releases code, training data and a fine‑tuned model, indicating immediate usability. The approach can be integrated into existing LLM pipelines and marketed as a security service for organizations deploying LLMs, making monetisation feasible within 90 days.

case_studies.title: ACCT: Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer
case_studies.abstract: In real-world deployments, large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly evolving from single-model invocation toward heterogeneous deployments in which different models are dynamically invoked for inference. When the same context is reused across models, however, each newly selected target model typically has to process it again, repeatedly incurring substantial computational costs. Therefore, we propose ACCT (Asymmetric Cross-LLM Context Transfer), which targets KV cache transfer between models of different scales within the same model family. ACCT transforms the KV cache produced by a source model into sparse KV states that can be directly consumed by a target model, thereby enabling cross-model reuse of context computation and decoupling context computation from downstream inference. ACCT consists of three lightweight components: the Cartographer identifies query-relevant context tokens for each target layer and KV head; the Allocator determines how many context tokens each target layer and KV head retains under a shared total KV budget; and the Compiler transforms selected source KV into sparse target KV. The target model can therefore perform inference using the transferred KV without reprocessing the original context. We evaluate ACCT in two complementary settings comprising five general-capability benchmarks and six highly context-dependent tasks. Experiments show that ACCT matches or exceeds the target model's original inference performance even when reducing the KV cache size by 75%. At a context length of approximately 19K tokens, ACCT's KV conversion achieves a 6.5-21.2 times speedup over target context prefill. These results demonstrate the feasibility of transferring context computation across models under a limited KV budget.
case_studies.summary: ACCT lets you move the key‑value cache (the context) from a smaller LLM to a larger one without re‑running the original prompt, saving up to 20× faster inference and cutting memory use by 75%. They built three light components that pick useful tokens, decide how many to keep, and convert the cache into a format the target model can use. The result is that the larger model can infer faster and with fewer tokens, matching or beating its usual performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage multi‑model LLM deployments, step 1: identify which models in your stack can be paired for cross‑cache transfer; step 2: apply a KV selector to keep only the most relevant context tokens within your budget; step 3: convert and load the sparse KV into the target model before inference. This can cut inference time and memory in your cloud infra.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete technique for reducing KV cache recomputation across LLMs, which directly benefits infrastructure engineers managing large LLM workloads on cloud platforms. It is a practical, algorithmic contribution with potential for immediate deployment in cost‑sensitive settings. However, the work appears to be a research prototype with no publicly released code or proven production deployment, so its maturity is moderate. The monetisation potential is reasonable because the method could be packaged as a cost‑savings tool or service for enterprises running heterogeneous LLM pipelines, but it is not a turnkey product yet. Overall, the paper scores well on real‑world impact and monetisation potential, but lower on maturity.

case_studies.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking
case_studies.abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.
case_studies.summary: Flide is an inference engine that speeds up decision‑making models by avoiding redundant calculation and keeping results mathematically exact. It does this by flattening token streams and using GPU‑based indices to fork attention across different decision branches, allowing up to 9.5× faster queries than existing engines while maintaining precision. This means faster, more accurate LLM‑driven decision systems for applications that need low latency and high reliability.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based decision systems, step 1: replace your current inference engine with Flide; step 2: update your deployment to use the flattened token stream format; step 3: test performance and precision against your baseline, aiming for up to 9.5× speed improvement without sacrificing accuracy.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Flide offers significant speed-ups for decision-based LLM agents, directly impacting infrastructure workloads that rely on rapid inference. However, the paper appears to present a prototype rather than a production-ready system, so maturity is modest. The solution could be adopted by engineers within 90 days, but would require integration work; thus monetisation potential is moderate.
